boundary_findings.what_the_value_spans: Starts in preview_theme_draft (theme_editor.rs:308) inside the 7th key's InputEvent::Change handler, after hex parsing, sync_picker and readability_issues. The first draft of a frame applies in that handler: apply_appearance runs at theme_editor.rs:309, one line after the stamp, and Palette::apply and apply_text_sizes call window.refresh() (appearance.rs:897 and 151). The handler then registers a next-frame callback (theme_editor.rs:317) which applies any draft coalesced from later edits in the same frame and registers trace_next_frame (main.rs:1326); the line prints from that second callback. The value therefore spans apply_appearance, the layout, paint and present of the whole-window render that shows the draft, and the wait for the frame request that prints the line. It excludes pre-handler input delivery (key 7 after XSync to the stamp: see key7_to_stamp_ms), OS presentation and completed GPU execution.
boundary_findings.includes_the_draw: Yes. Unlike a Settings switch, which applies in its handler and ends at the first next-frame callback before that frame is drawn, an editor edit always contains one whole-window draw. Measured directly in the 20 of 60 attribution edits whose draft render went through request_frame: the render started a median 0.75 ms after the stamp, took a median 20.352 ms of draw+present, and the line followed a median 5.956 ms after it. In the other 40 the same UI-thread CPU was spent with no 'frame duration' line, i.e. in the one production draw outside measure() that is reachable here (see attribution_method).
boundary_findings.difference_from_earlier_builds: The boundary is unchanged from cd563f6 and stated identically in metrics.md, which this build does not touch. On bb9f332 the apply was deferred to the first next-frame callback, so 34 of 60 edits first rendered the typed character in the old palette and then rendered the draft: two whole-window renders inside one value. From cd563f6 on, the apply precedes the keystroke's own render, so there is one render per edit and no old-palette frame between the stamp and the line.
boundary_findings.metric_catalogue: docs/benchmarks/metrics.md is byte-identical to cd563f6's and states the edit boundary: 'The custom theme editor prints the same name once per open and once per burst of live-preview edits (theme_editor::preview_theme_draft), with its own edit boundary: from the edit handler through the frame that shows the draft.' The catalogue describes the draft being painted by the frame that follows the first callback; on this host the paint is as often the keystroke's own synchronous render, which is inside the same span.
boundary_findings.x11_timer: gpui-pre-linux 0.3.4 x11/client.rs start_refresh_loop re-arms at the next 8.334 ms grid instant after a tick's work; trace lines landed on one grid (phase summary below)

dominant_cost.statement: One whole-window render at 2x of the Settings page with the editor dialog over it: a median 20.352 ms of draw+present (attribution launch) and a median 23.37 ms of UI-thread CPU per edit (recorded launch; 23.048 ms in the attribution launch). The palette application is the small remainder: the median per-edit CPU difference from the key-6 control is 1.847 ms in the recorded launch and 0.987 ms in the attribution launch, i.e. of order 1-2 ms.
evidence: UI-thread CPU for an edit is close to the key-6 control, a keystroke that changes the same text and renders the same rows but parses no valid colour and applies nothing: 23.37 vs 22.462 ms median in the recorded launch (median per-edit difference 1.847 ms) and 23.048 vs 22.386 ms in the attribution launch (median difference 0.987 ms).

60 of 60 attribution edits spent that CPU in exactly one continuous burst >= 1 ms (key7_bursts_ge_1ms_count): the handler, the apply and the render are one continuous piece of UI-thread work, with no gap in which a second render or a worker hand-off could sit.
Measured draft renders (20) cost 20.352 ms median and measured key-6 renders (22) cost 21.28 ms median: the render costs the same whether or not the palette changed.
Whole-process CPU per edit (23.668 ms median) is within 0.298 ms of the UI thread's, so no worker did the work and no job was submitted.
dominant_cost.residual: Beyond the render, the value holds the wait for the frame request that prints the line (draft_end_to_line_ms, median 5.956 ms) and the apply itself (of order 1-2 ms, from the key-6 control).

same_day_cd563f6_remeasurement.why: The cd563f6 record was measured earlier the same day under lighter host load (its four launches began at load averages 0.63-0.94, these at 0.50-1.88). Statistics from different hours of an uncontrolled desktop are not like-for-like, so the cd563f6 executable was run again, unchanged, after this build's four launches, with the same driver, fixture and procedure.
same_day_cd563f6_remeasurement.finding: Re-measured today, cd563f6 is 0.875 ms slower at the median (30.385 vs 29.51) and 0.74 ms slower at p95 (37.25 vs 36.51) than this build's recorded launch, and its UI-thread CPU per edit is 3.11 ms higher (26.48 vs 23.37), i.e. the two builds swap order between hours. The editor polish in 3927b57 therefore has no cost that this harness can resolve; the difference between the two records is host drift, not build.

comparison.noise_statement: The four 3927b57 launches span 1.203 ms of median and 1.001 ms of p95; the four cd563f6 launches spanned 2.047 ms and 1.929 ms. The criterion set's median differs from cd563f6's by 0.181 ms and its p95 by 1.357 ms, both inside those spreads, and the same-day re-measurement above puts cd563f6 on the slower side, so no difference between the two builds is resolvable with this harness. The bb9f332 gap is many times either spread.

attribution_method: Launch 'attribution-3927b57' set ZED_MEASUREMENTS=1, so gpui-pre-util 0.3.4 measure() printed 'frame duration' (Window::draw + present, window.rs:1781) for every frame drawn from request_frame, and sampled the UI thread's schedstat about every 1 ms. 20 of 60 edits produced such a line and 40 did not, while both groups spent the same UI-thread CPU and the same single burst. The only production draw outside measure() that a keystroke can reach is the synchronous flush at the top of Window::dispatch_key_event (window.rs:5606-5608), which draws a dirty window before dispatching the next key event; here the key-release of the same keystroke, after the handler applied the draft. So the draft render is that flush when it beats the frame timer and the measured frame otherwise. Draft-frame start = its line arrival - its duration; stamp = trace line arrival - printed value.
limitations: Linux XWayland on GNOME Wayland only (not native Wayland, not macOS); synthetic XTest keys through the X input method; 120 Hz display at 2x.
One recorded launch of 60 edits; warm caches; uncontrolled desktop load on the owner's active session.
The candidate is rebuilt after this evidence lands, so these numbers bind to executable sha256 1faff02061c9f07500cbf74827ae61d425d145caef6a153682230ef239bbe593 only.
No profiler on the host: costs are attributed to GPUI functions from frame-duration lines, CPU bursts and timing, not to app elements inside Window::draw.

One token (Canvas) edited through the hex field only; picker drags (the coalescing path) and edits that change the Readability list were not measured. The at-most-one-application-per-frame half of the criterion is covered by the task's test, not here.

This build's readability-count cache in the Your themes card is not exercised: the scratch store holds no custom themes, so the card renders 'No custom themes yet.' and the cached loop is empty in every frame measured here. The cache can only matter with saved custom themes, which this procedure never creates.
The no-compare control bounds the retained Split's share only to within launch-to-launch noise.
